meta.title: Who really said "The man who dies rich dies disgraced"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Carnegie really wrote it — closing his June 1889 essay “Wealth.” But the printed sentence reads “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The man who dies rich dies disgraced'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Carnegie, from “Wealth” (North American Review, June 1889, p. 664) — where the sentence carries one extra word: “thus.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. Carnegie wrote it to close “Wealth,” his essay in the North American Review of June 1889 — the piece the world now calls The Gospel of Wealth. The scanned page 664 reads “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced”; the popular form drops the “thus,” a shortening Carnegie himself made six months later.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Gospel of Wealth, and Other Timely Essays (Century, 1901)

source.excerpt: …yet the man who dies leaving behind him millions of available wealth, which was his to administer during life, will pass away “unwept, unhonored, and unsung,” no matter to what uses he leaves the dross which he cannot take with him. Of such as these the public verdict will then be: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”
trail: June 1889 — Carnegie publishes “Wealth” in the North American Review. The essay ends on page 664 ↗ with the line, set in quotation marks as the verdict a future public will pass.
December 1889 — the sequel, “The Best Fields for Philanthropy,” restates the sentence verbatim on page 685 ↗ — then, on page 698 ↗, Carnegie shortens it himself to “he who dies rich dies disgraced.”
1901 — the essays appear between covers as The Gospel of Wealth, and Other Timely Essays (Century), the edition scanned by the Internet Archive ↗, and the book title displaces the original one.
20 January 1914 — Carnegie records “The Gospel of Wealth” at the Edison Motion Picture Film Studio in the Bronx; the surviving audio ↗ is public domain, though the picture element is believed lost.
source.excerptNote: These are the closing lines of the essay, one sentence before Carnegie signs off. Note the two things the popular version loses: the word “thus,” and the fact that the sentence is quoted — Carnegie is forecasting a public verdict, not pronouncing one.

source.rightsNote: The sentence was first published in the North American Review in June 1889, and the collected book edition followed by 1901 — both far earlier than the 1931 threshold for U.S. public domain. Carnegie wrote in English, so no translation copyright is involved, and he died in 1919.

author.name: Andrew Carnegie
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Andrew Carnegie was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, emigrated to the United States as a boy, and built the steel business that made him one of the richest men alive. In 1889, while still amassing that fortune, he published a pair of essays arguing that a rich man is only a trustee of his surplus and must give it away during his own lifetime rather than bequeath it. He then spent the rest of his life doing it: by his death in 1919 his giving totalled roughly $350.7 million, funding libraries, universities and endowments on both sides of the Atlantic.

copyAttribution: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.” — Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review 148, no. 391 (June 1889): 664. The popular form drops the word “thus”; Carnegie used the shorter version himself in the December 1889 sequel.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in the quoting
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake. The unusual thing about “The man who dies rich dies disgraced” is that the real sentence is one word longer, and that missing word carries most of the argument.

items.who: “The man who dies rich dies disgraced”
items.why: The printed page 664 ↗ reads “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.” The “thus” refers back to the man Carnegie has just described, who dies “leaving behind him millions of available wealth, which was his to administer during life” — so the condemnation is of hoarding, not of wealth as such.

In the essay Carnegie does not pass the sentence himself. He predicts it: “Of such as these the public verdict will then be” — and encloses the line in quotation marks as the judgement he expects a future society to reach. The full text ↗ shows the setup clause.

The line is routinely credited to the book, but it began as a magazine article titled simply “Wealth,” published in the North American Review in June 1889 ↗. The essays were only gathered into a book later, as The Gospel of Wealth, and Other Timely Essays (Century, 1901 edition ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Before anyone else shortened it, Carnegie did. In the December 1889 sequel he refers in passing to “the doctrine that he who dies rich dies disgraced” — the “thus” already gone, on page 698 ↗. So the popular wording is his own abbreviation, not a stranger’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Carnegie published “Wealth” in 1889, at the height of the Gilded Age and while he was still building the fortune in question. Its argument was blunt: a rich man holds his surplus in trust for the community, should live without extravagance, and must distribute the money himself — because dying and leaving it behind is an abdication, not a gift. The closing sentence was the sting in the tail.

What makes the line unusual among famous quotations is that its author was tested by it. Carnegie sold his steel interests and spent his last two decades giving the proceeds away — libraries, universities, a hero fund, an endowment for international peace — a programme that, by his death in 1919, came to roughly $350.7 million.
detailsBody: On page 664 the sentence is not a blanket condemnation of wealth. The “thus” points backwards, to the man Carnegie has just described in the previous clause: one “who dies leaving behind him millions of available wealth, which was his to administer during life.” The disgrace attaches to the failure to administer, not to being rich.

Carnegie also puts the words in someone else’s mouth. He does not pronounce the verdict himself; he forecasts one — “Of such as these the public verdict will then be” — and sets the sentence inside quotation marks as the judgement a future society will pass.
context.pull: “Of such as these the public verdict will then be…”

sourcesVerified.claim: The closing page of Carnegie's essay "Wealth" — printed page 664 — reads: "Of such as these the public verdict will then be: 'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.'"
The full text of both 1889 essays contains the sentence three times, including the closing passage of Part I and the restatement in Part II.
On printed page 698 of "The Best Fields for Philanthropy" Carnegie writes of "the doctrine that he who dies rich dies disgraced" — the short form, without "thus".
On printed page 685 of "The Best Fields for Philanthropy" the sentence is restated verbatim as "The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced."

Wikiquote's sourced section gives the wording "The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced" with the citation: "Wealth," North American Review, June 1889, vol. 148, issue 391, p. 664. Carnegie's life dates are 25 November 1835 – 11 August 1919.
The Wikisource index for the scan gives the bibliographic details: "Wealth" by Andrew Carnegie, North American Review, volume 148, issue 391, June 1889.
The essay was originally titled "Wealth" and published in the North American Review in June 1889; it is more commonly known as "The Gospel of Wealth."
Andrew Carnegie was born 25 November 1835 and died 11 August 1919; he was Scottish-American, made his fortune in steel, and gave away approximately $350,695,653.

Project Gutenberg ebook 10253 is "The Gospel of Wealth by Andrew Carnegie," recorded January 20, 1914 at the Edison Motion Picture Film Studio, Bronx, New York; the motion picture element is believed lost.
The Internet Archive item is "The Gospel of Wealth, and Other Timely Essays" by Andrew Carnegie, published by Century, 1901.
Carnegie Corporation of New York's Gospel of Wealth page quotes the sentence in the form "The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced."
